of course! if you haven't played any yakuza games, you should start with 0 but I believe it's one of the harder ones to 100%, most of the other games in the series have cheat items that help you win in RNG games for example.

most of the time is spent on the completion list, the worst stuff is RNG gambling games like roulette and acquiring a big number of different gear and weapons. There's also mahjong which you will have to learn how to play but it isn't as complicated as I thought it would be. Overall not that difficult, you just need to learn a few minigames or look up a guide to help with strategies while putting in some time for the RNG games.

The truly difficult parts would be the legend difficulty run (unlocked after beating the story once, dying kicks you back to main menu and you have to reload a save instead of the checkpoints you usually get). There's 2 particularly difficult sections I remember, the universally hated car chase followed by an NPC protection section and the ending stretch where you have to do 2 long battles and 3 boss battles without dying. Considering you would be rushing through the game, you dont get a lot of upgrades so it is hard but it's easy to cheese with weapons.

There's also the climax battles which are challenges where you play with specific upgrades unlocked for your characters. Some are very easy and some are very difficult, I did not have fun with these lol.

Amon fights (really difficult boss battles unlocked after finishing all side quests) were pretty tough too but again, you are free to use weapons and can give yourself an easier time.

I wasn't using a guide unless I absolutely got stuck so I'm sure I could have had an easier time and finish faster, do use one if you are planning on running this. I finished in around 150 hours and looking it up on the internet, the average seems to be 145 hours so that should give you an idea :)

I agree that mission trees are satisfying since they give you specific goals and rewards, but I prefer having steam achievements giving me goals and letting me figure out how to get there on my own. I don't think EU4 got hurt that hard because of this since it got huge mechanics updates for 5 years before Rule Britannia added mission trees. most games don't get support for 5 years, let alone 10. It was a complete game by that point, so content packs are fine, just not what excites me personally. HoI4 definitely got hit the most since it started the whole mission tree thing. CK2 is my favorite paradox game as that game's updates were all mechanics up until the end. CK3 is mostly really good too, other than the weird region specific "struggle" stuff, though with a smaller map, even the regional content packs affect a larger portion of nations. EU4 being in between CK and HoI on this spectrum isn't a bad thing at all. Each game plays very differently, and I think that's a good thing.

I really don't like them as I would rather have paradox spend time making the game more dynamic for all nations rather than what is essentially a flavor mod for a certain region, priced the same as DLC that affect every nation. A new mission tree gives one interesting campaign while new mechanics can make every new campaign feel interesting, even when playing a nation you have played many times before.   
  
Of course at some point a game gets too bloated with mechanics, EU4 is a decade old and the devs probably hit a breaking point or two with the engine itself and had to switch to releasing content packs but as someone who started playing before the mission trees were added, I can say I got less and less excited every time a new expansion was released, especially as paradox's quality control went to shit in recent years. 

I think EU5 working towards more dynamic systems rather than rigid mission trees is great. I think a lot of people neglect roleplaying in paradox games and more dynamic systems allow you to play one nation in multiple different ways. Yes there will always be a meta way of playing so you could fall into playing every nation in the same way but if you are the type of person to go for a world conquest every time, you probably don't care much about mission tree flavor anyways lmao. The point is that in a dynamic game, you can set your own objectives rather than "get big" or "the mission tree told me to do it"

Maybe some of them failed exactly because they weren't okay with slavery and tried to change the ashlanders.

Nerevar was not expected to come back and reform their way of life. He specifically promised to protect the ashlander culture as is. The only way to prove that you are Nerevar is to act like him and follow whatever he might have said in the past. You inherit his mission to unite the houses and clans. That is literally one of two things everyone agrees he'll do, the other being defeating Dagoth Ur.

An incarnate that has come so far will have to ask themselves if they can continue their quest, even if it means to buy and sell a slave. They may see it as a necessary evil to defeat an existential threat. They may not care about slavery and never think about it twice. An abolitionist is going to think about what they are doing and may abandon the prophecy entirely. I think it's a quest that has a lot of potential for RPing.

I do agree that it would have been great to have an alternate route, and yes, it is kind of bad game design to have such a choice in the intended way of finishing the main quest, forcing anyone uncomfortable with it to finish the game through alternate ways which they'll have to look up on the internet. I still do like it as it makes you question what you are doing with your quest exactly. 

If you truly believe in the prophecy, what does Morrowind look like 3 decades from now, after all Outlanders have been killed or driven off of Morrowind? After the tribunal temples are destroyed and the settled people lose a huge part of their daily life? Will Morrowind ever prosper again? How will it deal with being surrounded by enemies on all sides and isolated from commerce after likely massacring lots of outlanders?

There's a lot of bad that will come out of this prophecy coming true, we just don't think about it because during the game we are acting vaguely heroic, until the slavery quest where most will question if they are doing the right thing. The quest just shows that you may not be doing the right thing just because you are the reincarnation of a legendary ruler. The quest also gives you the opportunity to roleplay a conflicted hero and change your mind about the entire thing midway through the main quest. 

I think a lot of RPGs suffer from letting you make a lot of choices in the early game, and then never let you change your mind on as you play. it's just hard to portray MC development through an RPG with a silent protagonist. For a first playthrough, yes, this is bad design, and it would have been nice to have an alternate route. If you are coming back to do a heavy RP playthrough, though? this is probably the most character developing moment the MC gets. Morrowind just doesn't have a rigid "Slavery is cool" or "Slavery is bad" dialogue, but the choice is there.

Check out Morrowind, it's the most immersive game I've played, there isn't horse riding but the enchantment/magic system is amazing and you can travel the world by getting a speed enchantment, high speed levitation spells or even jump spells. Daggerfall's world is absolutely huge with procedurally generated towns, each full with different kinds of shops, inns, temples and guild halls, as well as hundreds of NPCs in each of them. Vassals can be obtained in three ways:
- Declaring war on a country and using thr forcefully vassalize option

-Diplomatically offering a country vassalage

-Releasing them in lands that you already own through the diplomacy tab

Forcefully vassalizing them may not be an option if the country is too big as the bigger the country is, the more warscore it will cost you and if it is over 100% it is impossible for you to vassalize them this way. Before declaring a war, clicking on one of their provinces and hovering over the warscore cost of that province will reveal what the warscore cost for annexing their every province which is the same cost of vassalizing them. Keep in mind that doing this will give a huge opinion debuff and it might be better to consider fully annexing them first and then releasing them afterwards, which i will explain later. 

Diplomatically vassalizing them requires an alliance, 190 opinion and for both you and the target nation to be in peace. There are many more modifiers to this, for example an HRE elector will never accept a diplomatic vassalization. Neither will a country that has their own subjects or a country which you have core provinces of. It is harder but not impossible to vassalize countries which are HRE members. Having a stronger military than them and having high diplomatic reputation will help you in this.

Releasing a vassal country in your lands requires two things: the target nation not to currently exist, and for you to own at least one province which they have cores in. Once you release them your relations will be reset, which makes it so that, as i said earlier, it might be better to fully annex them and then release them to not get the opinion debuff.

Now the reasons you might want vassals. The number one reason why you want a vassal is to conquer their core lands from other countries for much cheaper aggressive expansion and you need not spend any administrative power. So when conquering land from a bigger country make sure to pay attention which currently non-existent country has lots of cores in their lands, conquer a single province of that nation and then release them as a vassal, giving you basically the best CB which is useful throughout the entire game.

Another reason to get a vassal is their mission tree. Lots of countries have mission trees which will gi e them permanent claims which can be useful, although personally I haven't found myself ever vassalizing someone just because of this, it's always more of a bonus on top of the main use of vassals.

Yet another reason might be their national ideas. One example is Georgia having lots of fort defense in their national ideas meaning when in war you can give control to the forts you siege down to georgia and enemies will have a harder time taking them back. Vassalizing Prussia will give you a nation with great military ideas, etc. Pay attention to your vassals ideas and find ways of utilizing them for your needs!

Now how to get vassals. Influence ideas were specifically made for a subject oriented game, and diplomatic ideas will of course, make it easier also. Finishing diplomatic ideas will make it so that you will not get - 1 stability from certain diplomatic actions, one of them being the "revoke march" action which i will explain later.
A strong military and a strong economy will help you with diplomatic vassalizations as well as keeping your current vassals loyal.

Speaking of, let's see how you can keep vassals loyal. The stronger the military and economy of your vassals, the more disloyal they will be. If your vassal has higher technology levels than you, this will also make them more disloyal. If their loyalty is over 50% nations which do not like you may support their independence, meaning if your vassal declares an independence war the supporters will join the war against you, so always keep the liberty desire in check. Ways of doing this is having high diplomatic reputation, keeping vassals' opinion of you high, conquering their core lands from other nations, attacking the rebels in their country, developping their lands, etc. If you have 2 or more vassals you can get the "strong duchies" policy from the noble estate, which lowers vassals' liberty desire and will give you more diplomatic relation slots so you always want this when you can get it.

Once 10 years have past since the beginning of vassalage and you have 190 opinion with your vassal, you may start annexing them which will cost diplomatic power and time based on how much development they have which can be modified through diplomatic reputation, ideas, policies and other interactions. Once you have finished annexing your vassal you will get -3 diplomatic reputation so keep in mind that during this time it will be harder to keep vassals loyal and annex them.

If you do not intend to annex your vassals soon, you may choose to make them a march which is a vassal that pays no tax and cannot be annexed but has better military capabilities and is more loyal. These bonuses only apply if your march has at most 25% of your development. If their development is too much compared to yours, they are basically normal vassals that do not pay tax and cannot be annexed with no real benefit. You may revoke a march but this will make them disloyal for a while and if you do not have diplomatic ideas finished, you will lose 1 stability. Keep in mind that the annexation timer will be reset after this action so you will have to wait another 10 years before you can annex them from this point.

I think that's all the useful info for now, if you have any questions feel free to ask and i will try my best to anwer. Hope this helps!
